title: Bank Balance Sheets
short: Assets (reserves, loans, securities) equal liabilities (deposits) plus owners' equity; reserves split into required and excess.
trouble: Students list deposits as a bank's assets. To the bank, a deposit is money it owes the depositor.

blocks.html: Most money in M1 is not cash but bank deposits. To see how banks handle them, economists use a simple balance sheet called a T-account.

A bank's assets (what it owns: reserves, loans, securities) equal its liabilities (what it owes: mainly customers' deposits) plus owners' equity. Reserves split into required reserves (reserve ratio × deposits) and excess reserves (everything above that).

When you deposit \$100, the bank owes you \$100 on demand: to the bank, your deposit is a liability. The \$100 of cash it now holds is an asset, a reserve. Both sides rise by \$100, so the T-account still balances. Whatever the bank does next (lend, buy a bond), it only swaps one asset for another or changes both sides together; that is why assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Equity is the cushion that belongs to the bank's owners.

blocks.cap: A bank's T-account with a 10% reserve requirement. Try "Customer deposits cash" and watch both sides change by the same amount.

blocks.title: Required and excess reserves
blocks.q: A bank has \$50,000 of deposits and \$8,000 of reserves. The reserve requirement is 10%.
steps: Excess reserves $= 8{,}000 - 5{,}000 = 3{,}000$ dollars, which the bank could lend.

blocks.title: Owners’ equity
blocks.q: A bank has reserves of \$6,000, loans of \$30,000 and securities of \$12,000, with deposits of \$44,000. Find equity.

blocks.html: A note on today's rules: the Federal Reserve set reserve requirements to zero in March 2020, so U.S. banks now have no required reserves. Problems here use a made-up ratio to show how the textbook model works; banks still hold reserves to make payments and to meet other regulations.

Listing deposits as a bank's assets. To the bank, a deposit is money it owes the depositor: a liability. The matching asset is the cash or reserves it holds. Check: both sides of a T-account must change by the same total.
